original_question: Is recognizing unit bar visibility graphs an NP-complete problem?
target_in_paper: Section 3.3, Open Problem 18: "Is recognition of unit bar visibility graphs NP-complete?"
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the exact open problem in the paper almost verbatim. It correctly asks about the recognition problem, correctly targets unit bar visibility graphs specifically, and correctly asks for NP-completeness rather than a broader characterization or reconstruction problem.
missing_details: The input should be stated explicitly: an arbitrary finite graph G.
The term "recognition" should be unpacked as a decision problem: decide whether G belongs to the class of unit bar visibility graphs.
A unit bar visibility graph should be defined from the nearby context: vertices are represented by pairwise disjoint horizontal bars in the plane, all of the same length.
The adjacency rule should be stated: two vertices are adjacent exactly when their corresponding bars have an unobstructed vertical line of sight.
The scope should be made explicit as the general class of unit bar visibility graphs, not only the special subclasses for which partial characterizations are known.
refined_question: Given a finite graph G, is it NP-complete to decide whether G is a unit bar visibility graph; that is, whether G admits a bar visibility representation by pairwise disjoint horizontal line segments in the plane, all of identical length, such that two vertices of G are adjacent if and only if their corresponding bars have an unobstructed vertical line of sight?
justification: The draft is already extremely close to the paper's official formulation. In Section 3.3, p. 18, the survey states Open Problem 18 exactly as the question of whether recognition of unit bar visibility graphs is NP-complete. The immediately preceding context in Section 3.3 defines bar visibility graphs via disjoint horizontal bars and then introduces unit bar visibility graphs by imposing the equal-length restriction on all bars; that is the precise local meaning your stand-alone rewrite must retain. The paper also uses "recognition problem" earlier in Section 2.1, p. 3, in the usual decision-problem sense of determining whether a given graph arises from the specified visibility model. No ambient ring/field, degree, homogeneity, nilpotency, operator, or asymptotic quantifier is relevant here, because this is a finite graph-recognition problem rather than an algebraic one.
